summary: Citizens of around 100 visa-exempt countries — including the EU, US, UK, Canada and Australia — can visit Israel for up to 90 days but must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorisation before boarding; other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli consulate, and nationals of several states with no relations with Israel are effectively barred.

notes: Duty-free allowances include 1 litre of spirits and 2 litres of wine per adult.
Drones must be declared and require Civil Aviation Authority approval — undeclared drones are confiscated.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted virtually everywhere, including buses and markets; a little cash is useful for small falafel stands and shared taxis (sherut).

safety.text: Israel is a modern, orderly country, but the security situation can change quickly: government advisories warn particularly about areas near Gaza and the Lebanese border, and rocket alerts can occur elsewhere. Learn how Home Front Command alerts work, follow local instructions, and check your government's advisory before and during your trip.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Israel, the West Bank and Gaza Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and autumn offer warm, dry weather for Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and the Galilee; the Dead Sea and Eilat are winter destinations, while July–August is hot and crowded.

tips.text: Israel does not stamp passports at Ben Gurion Airport and most crossings — you receive a small blue entry card instead. Keep it: hotels use it to grant VAT-exempt rates and you may be asked to show it at checkpoints or on departure.

Crossing overland from Jordan: the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge leads into the West Bank, has restricted hours (closing early on Fridays, Saturdays and holidays) and does not serve every category of traveller — the Jordan River crossing in the north and the Yitzhak Rabin crossing near Eilat are often simpler.
Expect detailed security questioning and bag screening at Ben Gurion Airport on departure — arrive at least 3 hours before your flight.
From Friday afternoon to Saturday nightfall (Shabbat) public transport largely stops outside Haifa and many businesses close — plan intercity travel around it.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Israel?
faq.answer: If you are from one of the roughly 100 visa-exempt countries — the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia, most of Latin America and others — you do not need a visa for stays of up to 90 days, but you must obtain an ETA-IL electronic travel authorisation online before boarding. All other nationalities need a B/2 visitor visa from an Israeli embassy or consulate.

faq.question: What is ETA-IL and how do I get one?
faq.answer: ETA-IL is Israel's electronic travel authorisation, mandatory for visa-exempt visitors. Apply at israel-entry.piba.gov.il with your passport details; the fee is ILS 25 per traveller and approval usually arrives within a day or two, though allow longer. It is valid for two years (or until your passport expires) and covers multiple visits of up to 90 days.

faq.question: Does Israel stamp your passport?
faq.answer: No — at Ben Gurion Airport and most border crossings you receive a slip of paper (entry card) instead of a stamp, precisely so your passport carries no Israeli evidence. Be aware, though, that exit stamps from Egyptian or Jordanian land borders adjacent to Israel can still reveal the visit to countries that refuse entry to travellers who have been to Israel.

faq.question: Will visiting Israel prevent me from entering other countries?
faq.answer: Some countries — including Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Libya and Yemen — refuse entry to travellers with evidence of a visit to Israel. Israel's paper entry card means your passport is normally clean, but land-border stamps from Jordan or Egypt can give the trip away. If you plan onward travel to such countries, sequence your trips or carry a second passport if your nationality allows it.

faq.question: Is it safe to visit Israel right now?
faq.answer: Conditions vary with the regional situation. Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and the main tourist areas function normally most of the time, but government advisories warn against areas near Gaza and the northern border, and rocket alerts can occur with little notice. Check your government's current advice, buy insurance that covers the situation, and follow Home Front Command instructions while in the country.
